newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-ECNZ split a pre-cursor to sale-Bradford.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ECNZ split a pre-cursor to sale-Bradford.

text.p: Plans to further split state-owned Electricity Corp of New Zealand lead naturally to privatisation, Energy Minister Max Bradford said on Wednesday.
Bradford told Reuters he was not about to break the government coalition agreement not to sell ECNZ and Contact Energy, identified as strategic assets.

"But what is clear is that at some point in the future, and this may be years away, the whole issue about ECNZ being a strategic asset comes into question as it becomes smaller and state generation becomes less dominant in the generation market," he said.
"I know that won't be a popular thought but inside five years the private sector will be generating about a third of our total electricity needs.

"You may well have between three and 'N' state-owned generators all competing in the marketplace and I'm not sure that we are terribly good at doing that kind of thing as government. It's a question then of should we own them."
Labour Party opposition spokesman on energy Pete Hodgson said a split of ECNZ made privatisation inevitable.

"It is not a matter of if, but when. Energy Minister Max Bradford is already softening up his coalition partner by pointing out that the more that ECNZ is split the less stratgic any of the baby ECNZ's will become," he said.
After a NZ$15 billion privatisation programme from 1987, the state generators are the jewells left in the government's crown.
ECNZ has total assets of $3.5 billion and Contact, which was split off from ECNZ with one third of its assets in 1995, has total assets of $1.4 billion.
Treasurer Winston Peters announced the plan to further split ECNZ in last month's budget as a move to enhance competition in the electricity market.
Bradford said the split would be a key ingredient of a package likely for introduction around the end of the year.
"Unless the wholesale price of electricity comes down as a first step, then consumers are not going to get the benefit at all," said Bradford, who is one of cabinet's 'drier' ministers.
He is also determined that benefits of lower wholesale prices will not be hogged by power distribution companies currently engaged in takeover mania.
Firstly, he wants consumers to get more information about the true costs of pricing of lines, and energy costs, and for that Bradford is pinning hopes on advancing metering technology.
His package will introduce disclosure regulations which would compel power companies to publish information more regularly -- separating costs of lines and energy business.
This is designed to stop companies cross subsidising parts of their businesses. But even Bradford is unsure of the efficacy of New Zealand's light-handed regulation approach to this.
"I'm a little sceptical that it will do it sufficiently well from a consumers' point of view."
He is also considering requiring power companies to split up their line, energy and metering businesses into separate companies to ensure true costs for each part are charged.
The speed of introduction of the package partly depends on ECNZ's attitude but a carrot to entice it would be to remove the ban on state power generators selling directly to consumers.
"It might set the cat among the pigeons but I certainly wouldn't contemplate doing that with ECNZ being the dominant player in the marketplace that it is now," Bradford said.
He has generally been happy with the opening of New Zealand's electricity market to competition begun in earnest last year, but he wants greater benefits passed on to consumers.
"The problems have been at the retail end. That is why I have taken such a strong line on this to ensure that competition did get down to the consumers.
"The government is determined to ensure that the retail power companies aren't in a position to block the development of proper competition," said Bradford.

"If there are signs that they are doing that -- that they are sitting behind local monopolies or near monopolies -- then the Commerce Act is there to do it, then I will have no compunction as minister in removing those barriers."
